final_task_tree.title: Research compliance across 50 states
final_task_tree.description: We're shipping a consumer mobile app that scans a user's face to verify identity at signup, and we charge a monthly subscription. Before launch I need to know, state by state, which biometric privacy laws apply to us, what notice and written consent we have to collect, how long we're allowed to retain the scan, whether there's a private right of action, and what the penalties are. Flag the states that are genuinely dangerous to launch in.

comments.body:
Starting. Scoping note on how I'm reading this brief, so you can correct me early if I've got it wrong:

Your product has three fact patterns that each trigger different law:
1. **Face scan for identity verification** → biometric privacy statutes (IL BIPA, TX CUBI, WA HB 1493, CO/TX/etc. sensitive-data rules under comprehensive privacy laws), plus facial-recognition-specific rules.
2. **Consumer mobile app collecting sensitive personal data** → the ~20 comprehensive state privacy laws, which almost all classify biometrics as "sensitive data" requiring opt-in consent and a data protection assessment.
3. **Monthly subscription** → automatic-renewal / negative-option laws (CA ARL, NY, and the federal FTC click-to-cancel rule). Not biometrics, but it's the other thing that generates class actions against subscription apps, so I'm flagging it rather than ignoring it.

A true 50-state matrix where 30 states have no biometric statute at all is mostly empty rows, so I'm structuring the deliverable as: tiered risk buckets + a full 50-state table + deep dives on the states that can actually hurt you. Breaking it into subtasks now.
comments.author: agent

comments.body:
Research done, report attached. Headline answers to your five questions:

**Which laws apply:** 4 dedicated biometric regimes (IL BIPA, TX CUBI, CO § 6-1-1314, WA — see below) + 20 comprehensive privacy laws that all treat biometrics as sensitive data + a subscription/auto-renewal layer. 28 states and DC have nothing biometric-specific.

**Notice and written consent:** build to Illinois BIPA § 15(b) and you clear all 50. Written notice of collection, written notice of specific purpose *and* specific duration, and a written release before capture. Electronic signature is valid since the 2024 amendment, so an in-app flow works.

**Retention:** the binding ceiling is Illinois — purpose satisfied *or* 3 years since last interaction, whichever is first — and Texas's 1-year-after-purpose-expires. My strong recommendation is to hold the template for zero days: verify, delete within 24h, keep a `verified: true` flag.

**Private right of action:** only Illinois, Washington (via MHMD/CPA), and California (breach only). Everywhere else is AG-enforced. That distinction is the whole risk map.

**Penalties:** IL $1k/$5k per person + fees; TX $25k per violation; CO $20k; CA $100–750 per consumer per breach; most Tier-3 states $7,500.

**Genuinely dangerous:** Illinois, Texas, Washington, California — but none of them is a no-go. Three things you probably didn't expect:

1. **Colorado is a second BIPA and nobody knows it.** HB 24-1130 applies regardless of volume thresholds, needs consent plus a public policy that includes breach response. Most compliance checklists miss it entirely.
2. **Washington's dedicated biometric statute probably doesn't apply to you** — it excludes data derived from photographs and only covers marketing-related "commercial purpose." Your Washington risk is the My Health My Data Act instead, which is the one with the private right of action.
3. **You have a hard pre-launch legal gate you may not have budgeted for:** the CCPA risk assessment under 11 CCR § 7150(a) must be *complete before your first California face scan*, not filed later.

Also flagged, since you're charging monthly: the FTC click-to-cancel rule was vacated nationwide in July 2025, but ~30 states have equivalents with private rights of action. Build the subscription flow to California AB 2863 and you're covered. Keep that consent **separate** from the biometric consent — one combined checkbox violates both statutes at once.

**Status: `needs_review`.** I've left 14 subtasks. The four I'd action first:
- **DECIDE the retention question** — blocks the consent screen copy, since BIPA makes you state the retention term on screen
- **DECIDE Illinois day-one** — my recommendation is yes, after the build lands
- **CCPA risk assessment** — gates California launch
- **Book counsel** — three questions genuinely need an opinion, and the load-bearing one is whether MHMD reaches identity-verification biometrics. That's untested and it determines whether you face class actions in Washington.

One thing I could not resolve and did not guess at: whether conditioning signup on biometric consent survives the "freely given" requirement in the comprehensive statutes. Shipping an alternative verification path largely sidesteps the question — I've made that a decision subtask rather than assuming your answer.
comments.author: agent

report.markdown:
# Biometric Privacy Compliance: 50-State Launch Assessment

**Product:** consumer mobile app, face scan for identity verification at signup, monthly subscription
**Date of research:** 6 August 2026
**Bottom line:** there is no state you must avoid. There are four states that will punish a sloppy launch, and one build that satisfies all of them. The real risk is not geography — it is shipping before the consent screen, deletion job and published retention policy exist.

> Not legal advice. This is a research memo to direct counsel's attention efficiently, not to replace them. Three items genuinely need an outside opinion and they are flagged as such.

---

## 1. The answer in one page

**Genuinely dangerous to launch in — 4 jurisdictions.** These are the only places where a private plaintiff can sue you, which is what turns a compliance error into a class action.

| State | Why it's dangerous | Worst case |
|---|---|---|
| **Illinois** | BIPA — broad private right of action, no injury required, attorneys' fees, 5-year lookback | $1,000/person negligent, $5,000/person reckless, plus fees |
| **Texas** | No private right of action, but the AG is the most aggressive biometric regulator in the country | $25,000 **per violation**; Meta settled a CUBI action for **$1.4B**, Google for **$1.375B** |
| **Washington** | My Health My Data Act — private right of action via the Consumer Protection Act; biometric data is enumerated as "health" data | Treble damages capped at $25k + fees, per plaintiff, plus AG action |
| **California** | Private right of action **only for a data breach** — but biometric data is an enumerated trigger, so one breach = automatic class action | $100–$750 **per consumer per incident**, no proof of harm needed |

**Sleeper states most people miss:**
- **Colorado** — HB 24-1130 (§ 6-1-1314, effective 1 Jul 2025) is effectively a second BIPA. It applies to **any** controller processing biometric identifiers **regardless of volume thresholds**, requires consent and a public retention/destruction/**breach-response** policy. No private right of action, $20k per violation. Almost nobody has this on their map.
- **Maryland** — MODPA is the strictest data-minimisation law in the US. Sensitive data may only be processed when **strictly necessary** to the service the consumer requested, and **consent cannot override this**. Sale of sensitive data is banned outright even with consent.

**The threshold trap.** Most of the 20 comprehensive privacy laws only bite above ~100,000 residents, so a launching app is below threshold in most states on day one. But **Illinois, Texas CUBI, Colorado § 6-1-1314 and Washington MHMD have no threshold at all** and apply from your first user. Do not let anyone conclude you are too small to be covered.

---

## 2. Tiered map of all 51 jurisdictions

**Tier 1 — private right of action (4):** Illinois, Washington, California (breach only), plus New York City's local ordinance — which has a private right of action but applies to physical "commercial establishments" (retail, food, entertainment) and almost certainly **does not reach a mobile app**.

**Tier 2 — dedicated biometric statute, regulator-enforced only (3):** Texas (CUBI, $25k/violation), Colorado (§ 6-1-1314, $20k/violation), Washington (RCW 19.375, $7,500 — see §4, probably inapplicable to us).

**Tier 3 — comprehensive privacy law, biometrics = sensitive data, opt-in consent, AG-enforced (17 more):** Virginia, Connecticut, Utah, Oregon, Florida, Montana, Delaware, Iowa, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Tennessee, Minnesota, Maryland, Indiana, Kentucky, Rhode Island.

**Tier 4 — no biometric-specific and no comprehensive law (28 states + DC):** AL, AK, AZ, AR, GA, HI, ID, KS, LA, ME, MA, MI, MS, MO, NV, NM, NY, NC, ND, OH, OK, PA, SC, SD, VT, WV, WI, WY, DC. Governed by breach-notification statutes and state UDAP laws — **most UDAP statutes do carry private rights of action**, so a "your consent flow was deceptive" theory remains available even here. Your privacy policy promises are the exposure.

Full state-by-state table with consent standards, retention limits, private-right-of-action status and penalties is in the subtask **"Build the full 50-state classification table."**

### Comprehensive privacy law effective dates
CA 2020 · VA 1 Jan 2023 · CO 1 Jul 2023 · CT 1 Jul 2023 · UT 31 Dec 2023 · TX 1 Jul 2024 · OR 1 Jul 2024 · FL 1 Jul 2024 · MT 1 Oct 2024 · DE 1 Jan 2025 · IA 1 Jan 2025 · NE 1 Jan 2025 · NH 1 Jan 2025 · NJ 15 Jan 2025 · TN 1 Jul 2025 · MN 31 Jul 2025 · MD 1 Oct 2025 · IN, KY, RI all 1 Jan 2026.

Notable: **Florida** only reaches companies over $1B revenue (ignore it). **Rhode Island** has the lowest threshold in the country at 35,000 consumers. **Connecticut** drops from 100,000 to 35,000 in July 2026. **Oregon's** cure period expired January 2026 — assume no free first bite anywhere.

---

## 3. Notice and consent: what you actually have to collect

Build to the Illinois standard and you clear every state. BIPA § 15(b) requires, **before** collection:

1. Written notice that a biometric identifier is being collected and stored
2. Written notice of the **specific purpose AND the length of term** of collection, storage and use
3. A **written release** executed by the subject

The second element is where most flows fail. "We keep your data as long as necessary" does not satisfy § 15(b)(2) — you must state a concrete period on screen.

**Good news from the 2024 amendment (SB 2979):** "written release" now expressly includes **electronic signature**, so an in-app consent flow is valid. No wet signature.

**Design rules that follow from the strictest states:**
- Standalone screen. Not the ToS, not the privacy policy, not a pre-ticked box.
- Name the ID-verification vendor and disclose transmission to them (BIPA § 15(d), MHMD sharing consent).
- Decline button equally prominent — **dark patterns invalidate consent** under Washington MHMD and several comprehensive laws.
- **Two separate consents**: biometric, and subscription auto-renewal. One combined checkbox breaks BIPA (needs a standalone release) and California AB 2863 (needs unbundled renewal consent) *simultaneously*.
- Do not geo-gate the consent flow by IP. Residency governs, not location at signup, and residents travel.

**California is the one opt-out state.** CCPA treats biometric info as sensitive personal information but gives a *right to limit* rather than requiring opt-in. You still need notice at collection and the "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information" mechanism. Note that CCPA expressly treats photographs as biometric data **when used for facial recognition** — no photograph escape hatch.

---

## 4. Retention: how long you can hold the scan

| Regime | Ceiling |
|---|---|
| **Illinois** | Purpose satisfied **OR** 3 years since last interaction — **whichever is first** |
| **Texas** | No later than **1 year** after the purpose for collecting expires |
| **Illinois + Colorado** | Whatever your **published policy** says — failing to follow your own policy is itself a violation |
| **Maryland** | Only what is **strictly necessary**; consent cannot expand this |

**Strong recommendation: don't retain the template at all.** Verify, match, delete within 24 hours, keep only a non-biometric `verified: true` flag plus timestamp and method.

This is the highest-leverage decision in the project. If you hold no biometric data you largely escape BIPA's storage and security duties, CUBI's destruction obligations, and — most importantly — **the CCPA breach class action, which requires biometric data to actually be exfiltrated**. You cannot leak what you never kept. For an identity-verification-at-signup use case, "purpose satisfied" plausibly occurs the moment verification completes, so retention is hard to justify anyway.

---

## 5. Two findings that cut against the conventional wisdom

**Washington's dedicated biometric statute probably doesn't apply to you.** RCW 19.375 fails on two independent grounds: its definition of "biometric identifier" expressly excludes "a physical or digital photograph, video or audio recording **or data generated therefrom**" — so a faceprint derived from a selfie is arguably excluded outright; and it only bites on enrolment "for a **commercial purpose**", narrowly defined as furthering sale or disclosure to a third party for **marketing unrelated goods or services**. Verifying identity for your own signup is not that. Washington's real risk is entirely MHMD.

**MHMD's application to identity-verification biometrics is untested and it matters.** Biometric data is enumerated at RCW 19.373.010(8)(b)(ix) as a category of "physical or mental health status" — the plaintiff reading is that *all* biometric data is therefore consumer health data. The counterargument is that the umbrella definition still requires the data to identify health status. Nobody has litigated this to a conclusion. Because MHMD carries a private right of action, **get a written opinion** — it is one of the three questions worth paying counsel for.

---

## 6. The subscription layer (separate risk, same launch gate)

The FTC's "click-to-cancel" Negative Option Rule was **vacated nationwide** by the Eighth Circuit on 8 July 2025 (*Custom Communications v. FTC*) on procedural grounds. It never took effect. Do not build to it as a federal requirement and do not assume it preempts anything.

But roughly 30 states have equivalent statutes, mostly enforced through UDAP laws that **do** carry private rights of action — which is why auto-renewal claims are so common against subscription apps. **California AB 2863** (effective 1 Jul 2025) is the strictest, so build to it once nationally: unbundled clear-and-conspicuous consent covering free trials; retain consent proof 3 years or 1 year post-termination whichever is longer; annual reminder stating renewal frequency, amount and cancellation instructions; same-channel click-to-cancel with no obstruction.

The two items always missed: **durable consent-proof storage** and **the annual reminder job**.

---

## 7. Pre-launch gates, in order

1. **DECIDE the retention question** — everything else depends on it, including the consent screen copy
2. **CCPA risk assessment** — a hard legal gate, not a 2027 problem. Under 11 CCR § 7150(a) (effective 1 Jan 2026) it must be **complete before the first California scan**, because processing sensitive PI is "significant risk" processing. Producible to the CPPA within 30 days on request. Write it once and reuse it as the data protection assessment for the other comprehensive-law states
3. **Standalone consent screen** + **immutable consent-record store** (must survive BIPA's 5-year limitations period even after the biometric data is deleted)
4. **Automated deletion job with audit logging** — must match the published policy exactly
5. **Publish two documents**: the Biometric Data Retention & Destruction Policy (BIPA § 15(a) + Colorado, and Colorado requires a breach-response section), and — separately — the **standalone Washington Consumer Health Data Privacy Policy with its own homepage link**, which may not be merged into the main privacy policy. This is the single most commonly missed MHMD requirement
6. **Vendor contract flow-down** — first, ask the vendor in writing where templates are stored, for how long, and whether they train on them. Vendor default retention is a very common source of unknowing violation
7. **Counsel review** of the three open judgement calls

## 8. Hard prohibitions — no consent cures these

- **Never sell, lease, trade or profit from biometric data.** BIPA § 15(c), Colorado, Texas; Maryland bans sale of sensitive data outright even with consent
- **Never use the scans for model training or any secondary purpose.** Breaks purpose limitation everywhere and fails Maryland's "strictly necessary" test
- **Never disclose beyond the named vendor** without fresh consent

## 9. Watch list

BIPA-style bills **with private rights of action** are pending in **New York** (mirrors BIPA's $1,000/$5,000), **Massachusetts, Vermont, Maryland (HB 33), Kentucky, Mississippi, Missouri, Washington**. Two are product-breaking: the **Mississippi and Missouri** drafts would **prohibit conditioning provision of a service on biometric consent** — which is exactly what a mandatory face-scan signup does. Shipping a non-biometric alternative verification path both future-proofs against this and shores up the "freely given consent" argument today.

subtasks.title: Illinois BIPA — the launch-blocking statute
subtasks.description:
Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act, 740 ILCS 14. VERDICT: highest-risk state in the country for this product, but compliable. Do not launch in IL without all five items below shipped.

STATUTORY ELEMENTS (740 ILCS 14/15):
- 15(a) Must develop a WRITTEN, PUBLICLY AVAILABLE policy with a retention schedule + destruction guidelines. Destruction deadline = when initial purpose is satisfied OR 3 years after the individual's last interaction, WHICHEVER IS FIRST. For identity verification at signup, "purpose satisfied" arguably occurs the moment verification completes — this is the key design decision (see spec subtask).
- 15(b) Before collection you must (1) inform the subject IN WRITING that a biometric identifier is being collected/stored; (2) inform them IN WRITING of the specific purpose AND the length of term of collection/storage/use; (3) receive a WRITTEN RELEASE executed by the subject. All three are prerequisites to collection.
- 15(c) Absolute bar on selling, leasing, trading, or otherwise profiting from biometric data. No exceptions, no consent workaround.
- 15(d) No disclosure/redisclosure without separate consent (this covers your ID-verification vendor).
- 15(e) Reasonable standard of care in industry + protection at least as protective as how you treat other confidential info.

"Biometric identifier" expressly includes "scan of ... face geometry". The statute excludes "photographs", but case law (Rivera v. Google, Clearview litigation) treats a faceprint/geometry template DERIVED from a photo as covered. Do not rely on the photograph exclusion.

LIABILITY (740 ILCS 14/20): private right of action for "any person aggrieved". Liquidated damages $1,000 negligent / $5,000 intentional or reckless, or actual damages if greater, PLUS attorneys' fees and costs and injunctive relief. Fee-shifting is what drives the plaintiff bar. Rosenbach: no actual injury required — a bare procedural violation makes you "aggrieved". Statute of limitations 5 years for all BIPA claims (Tims v. Black Horse Carriers, 2023).

2024 AMENDMENT (SB 2979, effective Aug 2 2024) — two changes in your favour:
1. Damages capped at ONE recovery per person per type of violation for repeat collections of the same identifier from the same person by the same method (fixes Cothron per-scan accrual).
2. "Written release" now expressly includes ELECTRONIC SIGNATURE — an in-app e-signature consent flow is valid.
The Seventh Circuit held in 2026 that the damages amendment applies RETROACTIVELY to pending cases.

Exposure math even post-amendment: 100,000 IL signups x $1,000 negligent = $100M theoretical. The cap helps per-user, not per-class.

subtasks.title: Texas CUBI — AG enforcement, $25k per violation
subtasks.description:
Texas Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act (CUBI), Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001. VERDICT: no class-action risk, but the worst regulator risk in the country. Launchable with compliant flow.

SCOPE: "Biometric identifier" = retina/iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or RECORD OF HAND OR FACE GEOMETRY. A face scan for identity verification is squarely in scope. Note Texas has NO photograph exclusion in the definition, so it is broader than Washington's statute here.

REQUIREMENTS:
- May not capture a biometric identifier for a COMMERCIAL PURPOSE unless you first INFORM the person AND RECEIVE CONSENT. Texas does not require a signed "written release" like Illinois — notice + consent is enough, and consent can be inferred in some contexts, but written/affirmative in-app consent is the safe build.
- No sale/lease/disclosure except narrow exceptions (individual consents for disappearance/death identification; completes a financial transaction the individual requested or authorized; required by federal or non-Ch.552 state statute; law-enforcement warrant).
- Reasonable care in storage/transmission, at least as protective as other confidential information you hold.
- DESTROY within a reasonable time and NO LATER THAN THE FIRST ANNIVERSARY of the date the purpose for collecting expires. For signup ID verification, the purpose expires when verification completes — so the outside limit is 1 year from that point, and much sooner is defensible.

PENALTIES: civil penalty up to $25,000 PER VIOLATION. Texas AG has EXCLUSIVE enforcement authority — there is NO private right of action, so no class actions. But note the AG has treated "per violation" aggressively as per-person-per-image: the Meta CUBI action settled for $1.4 BILLION (largest ever by a single state), and the Google action settled for $1.375 billion. Texas is the highest-magnitude regulator risk in the US even though there is no plaintiff bar.

2025 AMENDMENT (HB 149 / TRAIGA, effective Jan 1 2026): amended CUBI to exempt biometric identifiers that the individual has made publicly available, and to carve out AI-training and certain security/law-enforcement uses. Does NOT help us — our capture is a direct, non-public collection from the user.

SEPARATE TEXAS OBLIGATION: the Texas Data Privacy and Security Act (TDPSA) also applies and treats biometric data as sensitive data requiring opt-in consent. Texas therefore has TWO overlapping regimes and no small-business revenue threshold in TDPSA. See the comprehensive-privacy-law subtask.

subtasks.title: Washington — HB 1493 plus the My Health My Data Act
subtasks.description:
Washington. Two statutes, and the surprising conclusion is that the DEDICATED BIOMETRIC LAW PROBABLY DOES NOT APPLY TO US while the HEALTH law probably does.

(1) RCW 19.375 (HB 1493, 2017) — LIKELY OUT OF SCOPE, two independent reasons:
- Definition: "biometric identifier" expressly EXCLUDES "a physical or digital photograph, video or audio recording OR DATA GENERATED THEREFROM". If our faceprint template is derived from a selfie image or video capture, it is arguably excluded outright. This is the opposite of Illinois, where courts rejected the photograph defence.
- Trigger: the prohibition only bites on enrolling a biometric identifier "for a COMMERCIAL PURPOSE", and commercial purpose is narrowly defined as furthering the sale or disclosure to a third party for MARKETING goods or services UNRELATED to the initial transaction. Using a face scan to verify identity for our own signup is not a commercial purpose.
- If it did apply: AG-exclusive enforcement via the Consumer Protection Act (RCW 19.375.030), up to $7,500 per violation. NO private right of action.
DO NOT rely on this analysis to skip consent — we are getting consent anyway for IL/TX, so the point is moot. Just don't panic about WA 19.375.

(2) MY HEALTH MY DATA ACT, RCW 19.373 — THIS IS THE REAL WASHINGTON RISK.
- "Biometric data" is expressly enumerated at RCW 19.373.010(8)(b)(ix) as an item within "physical or mental health status", which is what makes data "consumer health data". Plaintiffs read this to mean ALL biometric data is consumer health data regardless of any health connection. The counterargument (the umbrella clause still requires the data to identify health status) is untested. Assume it applies.
- "Biometric data" definition covers imagery of the face "from which an identifier template can be extracted" — no photograph exclusion here, unlike 19.375.
- Applies to entities that do business in WA or target products/services to WA individuals. No revenue or volume threshold — it catches startups.
- Requires: (a) SEPARATE consent before collecting consumer health data, obtained before collection, not bundled with the general privacy policy; (b) separate additional consent before SHARING; (c) a distinct WRITTEN AUTHORIZATION (with prescribed content) before any SALE; (d) a SEPARATE, standalone consumer health data privacy policy, linked on its own from the homepage — it may NOT be folded into the main privacy policy; (e) consumer rights to access, withdraw consent, and DELETE, with deletion flowing down to processors/affiliates; (f) binding processor contracts.
- "Consent" must be a clear affirmative act, freely given, specific, informed, opt-in, unambiguous; may be electronic. Consent obtained through DECEPTIVE DESIGN (dark patterns) is invalid.
- ENFORCEMENT: violation is a per se Consumer Protection Act violation, RCW 19.373.090, which carries a PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION. Plaintiff must prove the five WCPA elements including injury to business or property — the main defence, and the reason MHMD litigation has been slower to materialise than BIPA. Class actions have already been filed. Treble damages capped at $25,000 plus attorneys' fees under WCPA, plus AG enforcement.

NET: Washington is tier-1 risk because of MHMD, not because of its biometric statute. The extra build item unique to WA is the standalone consumer health data privacy policy with its own homepage link.

subtasks.title: Colorado + other comprehensive-privacy states: biometrics as sensitive data
subtasks.description:
Comprehensive state consumer privacy laws. 20 states in effect as of 2026. ALL of them classify biometric data as SENSITIVE DATA. In 19 of 20 (all but California) that means AFFIRMATIVE OPT-IN CONSENT is required before processing, plus a documented data protection assessment / risk assessment for processing sensitive data. None of them has a private right of action — all are AG-enforced.

THE THRESHOLD POINT THAT MATTERS MOST: most of these laws only apply above a volume threshold (typically 100,000 state residents, or 25,000 plus revenue from data sales). A pre-launch app is below threshold in most states on day one. BUT the dedicated biometric regimes (Illinois BIPA, Texas CUBI, Colorado § 6-1-1314, Washington MHMD) have NO threshold at all and apply from the very first user. Do not let anyone conclude "we're too small to be covered".

EFFECTIVE DATES (all AG-enforced):
CA CCPA/CPRA 2020 | VA CDPA 1 Jan 2023 | CO CPA 1 Jul 2023 | CT CTDPA 1 Jul 2023 | UT UCPA 31 Dec 2023 | TX TDPSA 1 Jul 2024 | OR OCPA 1 Jul 2024 | FL FDBR 1 Jul 2024 | MT MCDPA 1 Oct 2024 | DE DPDPA 1 Jan 2025 | IA ICDPA 1 Jan 2025 | NE NDPA 1 Jan 2025 | NH NHPA 1 Jan 2025 | NJ NJDPA 15 Jan 2025 | TN TIPA 1 Jul 2025 | MN MNDPA 31 Jul 2025 | MD MODPA 1 Oct 2025 | IN 1 Jan 2026 | KY 1 Jan 2026 | RI 1 Jan 2026.

THE OUTLIERS THAT CHANGE THE BUILD:

COLORADO — HB 24-1130, new CPA § 6-1-1314, effective 1 Jul 2025. This is effectively a second BIPA and is widely under-appreciated. It applies to ANY controller processing biometric identifiers REGARDLESS OF THE CPA's VOLUME THRESHOLDS. Requires: consent before collection; a publicly available written policy covering retention schedule, destruction guidelines AND breach response; a ban on selling/leasing/trading biometric identifiers; a consumer right to access their biometric data; and it extends to EMPLOYEE biometric data (unusual — the CPA otherwise excludes employment data). Enforced by the AG and district attorneys, penalties up to $20,000 per violation. NO private right of action. Treat Colorado as a near-BIPA state for build purposes.

MARYLAND — MODPA, effective 1 Oct 2025. Strictest data-minimisation regime in the country. (1) Sensitive data (incl. biometric) may only be collected/processed/shared when STRICTLY NECESSARY to provide or maintain a product or service the consumer specifically requested — consent is NOT a route around this, so we must be able to argue face scan is strictly necessary to the signup the user asked for (defensible for identity verification, indefensible for anything secondary like model training or fraud analytics on other products). (2) The SALE of sensitive data is PROHIBITED OUTRIGHT, consent cannot cure it — first state to do this. (3) MODPA broadens the biometric definition to data that "can be used to" uniquely authenticate identity, rather than data intended to be so used, catching grey-area cases.

TEXAS TDPSA and NEBRASKA NDPA — NO volume threshold. Applies to anyone doing business in the state or producing a product consumed by residents, unless a US SBA-defined small business. Even qualifying small businesses may NOT sell sensitive data without consent (TDPSA; Neb. Rev. Stat. 87-1118, up to $7,500 per violation). So the TDPSA sits on top of CUBI in Texas.

RHODE ISLAND — lowest threshold of any state: 35,000 consumers, or 10,000 if >20% of revenue comes from selling personal data. Will catch us earlier than most.

CONNECTICUT — threshold DROPS from 100,000 to 35,000 consumers from July 2026. Recalculate scope then.

OREGON — 30-day right to cure EXPIRED January 2026. No more free first bite.

FLORIDA FDBR — only reaches companies with revenue over $1B. Out of scope for us; effectively ignore.

CURE PERIODS: several states have let theirs sunset (incl. Oregon, and Colorado/Connecticut sunsets have passed). Do not plan around a cure period.

subtasks.title: California — CCPA/CPRA sensitive data + the ARL subscription trap
subtasks.description:
California. Moderate biometric risk, but a HARD PRE-LAUNCH GATE (risk assessment) and the country's worst subscription-billing exposure.

CCPA/CPRA — BIOMETRICS:
- Biometric information is SENSITIVE PERSONAL INFORMATION. California is the ONE outlier among the 20 comprehensive states: it does NOT require opt-in consent. Instead consumers get a RIGHT TO LIMIT the use and disclosure of sensitive PI, i.e. an opt-out. We still need the notice at collection, the "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information" mechanism, purpose limitation, and a stated retention period.
- Note the CCPA definition treats photographs as biometric data WHEN USED FOR FACIAL RECOGNITION PURPOSES — which is exactly our use case. No photograph escape hatch.
- PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION: narrow but real. Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.150 gives consumers a private action ONLY for a DATA BREACH caused by failure to maintain reasonable security. Statutory damages $100–$750 per consumer per incident, or actual damages. Critically, "unique biometric data used to identify a person" is one of the ENUMERATED data types that triggers this right. So a single breach of our faceprint store = a class action with per-consumer statutory damages and no need to prove harm. There is a 30-day notice-and-cure for this action, but a breach cannot be cured.
- Enforcement: CPPA and the AG. No cure period as of right since 2023.

*** PRE-LAUNCH GATE — CCPA RISK ASSESSMENT ***
New CPPA regulations took effect 1 Jan 2026. Under 11 CCR § 7150(a), a business must COMPLETE A RISK ASSESSMENT BEFORE INITIATING any processing activity involving "significant risk", and processing sensitive personal information is such an activity. Because we are launching after 1 Jan 2026, this is not a 2027 problem — the assessment must exist BEFORE the first California face scan. The CPPA or AG can demand a copy at any time and we must produce it within 30 days. Annual summary reporting to the CPPA begins 1 Apr 2028 (for assessments done in 2026–27, submit summary info, not the full assessment, by 1 Apr 2028). Cybersecurity audit obligations phase in 2028–2030 by revenue tier.
Also check ADMT: if the face match ever gates a "significant decision" (financial services, credit, housing, employment, essential goods), the ADMT rules add pre-use notice and opt-out rights. For a general consumer app, probably not triggered — but confirm with counsel if the product is fintech-adjacent.

AUTOMATIC RENEWAL LAW — AB 2863, in effect 1 Jul 2025. Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17600 et seq. This is the highest-frequency class-action risk for any subscription app, entirely separate from biometrics:
- Expanded to cover FREE TRIALS / "free-to-pay conversions" and negative-option programs.
- Consent for the auto-renewal must be obtained separately, clearly and conspicuously, and must NOT be bundled with other terms. Dark patterns invalidate consent.
- Must RETAIN PROOF of the consumer's affirmative consent for at least 3 years, or 1 year after termination, whichever is LONGER. Engineering requirement: log and archive the consent artifact.
- ANNUAL REMINDER notice stating renewal frequency, amount charged, and cancellation instructions.
- CLICK-TO-CANCEL: cancellation must be available through the SAME channel used to sign up, must be at least as easy as signing up, and online sign-ups need a cancel button. No obstruction or delay flows.
IMPORTANT INTERACTION: the ARL consent and the biometric consent must be TWO SEPARATE, UNBUNDLED consents. Bundling them breaks both statutes at once — BIPA requires a standalone release and the ARL requires unbundled renewal consent.

subtasks.title: Build the full 50-state classification table
subtasks.description:
FULL 51-JURISDICTION CLASSIFICATION (50 states + DC). Tiers:
T1 = private right of action exists (class-action risk)
T2 = dedicated biometric statute, regulator-enforced only
T3 = comprehensive privacy law only; biometrics = sensitive data, opt-in consent, AG-enforced
T4 = no biometric-specific or comprehensive law; breach-notification + UDAP only

| State | Tier | Regime | Consent standard | Retention limit | PRA | Penalty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Washington | T1 | My Health My Data RCW 19.373 (+RCW 19.375, likely inapplicable) | Separate opt-in consent before collection; separate consent to share; authorization to sell | Deletion on request, flows to processors | YES (via Consumer Protection Act) | CPA: treble up to $25k + fees; 19.375: $7,500 AG-only |
| California | T1 (breach only) | CCPA/CPRA; + ARL AB 2863 | Notice at collection + right to LIMIT (opt-out, not opt-in) | Must disclose retention period; purpose limitation | YES but ONLY for data breach | $100–$750 per consumer per breach incident; CPPA/AG penalties |
| Texas | T2 | CUBI § 503.001 + TDPSA | Inform + obtain consent before capture | No later than 1 yr after purpose expires | No | Up to $25,000 PER VIOLATION, AG exclusive (Meta $1.4B, Google $1.375B) |
| Colorado | T2 | CPA § 6-1-1314 (HB 24-1130) + CPA | Consent before collection; NO volume threshold | Public policy w/ retention + destruction + breach response | No | Up to $20,000 per violation; AG + district attorneys |

Governed by the state breach-notification statute and the state UDAP/consumer-protection statute (most UDAP statutes DO have private rights of action, so a deceptive-consent-flow theory is still available to plaintiffs) | Whatever your privacy policy promises — misrepresentation is the exposure | — | Via UDAP | Varies |

BREACH-NOTIFICATION STATUTES THAT EXPRESSLY COVER BIOMETRIC DATA (a breach here triggers notice duties even in T4 states): AZ, AR, CA, CO, DE, IA, IL, LA, MD, NE, NM, NY (SHIELD), NC, OR, RI, SD, WA, WI, WY. Assume the list keeps growing.

ARKANSAS NOTE: Arkansas has NO comprehensive privacy law. It enacted the Arkansas Children and Teens' Online Privacy Protection Act (HB 1717), effective 1 Jul 2026 — a COPPA-style law, AG-enforced, no PRA. Relevant only if we have minor users.

LEGISLATIVE WATCH LIST — BIPA-style bills WITH private rights of action have been introduced in NEW YORK (statutory damages $1,000/$5,000, mirrors BIPA), MASSACHUSETTS, VERMONT, MARYLAND (HB 33), KENTUCKY, MISSISSIPPI, MISSOURI and WASHINGTON. Two design-relevant features in some drafts: (a) NY and WA versions would also cover public-sector entities; (b) the MISSISSIPPI and MISSOURI drafts would BAR conditioning provision of a service on biometric consent — that would directly break a mandatory face-scan signup. Re-check this list each legislative session.

subtasks.title: Subscription / auto-renewal compliance layer
subtasks.description:
Subscription / auto-renewal layer. Not biometric law, but this is where consumer subscription apps actually get sued, so it belongs in the launch checklist.

FEDERAL: the FTC's Negative Option ("Click-to-Cancel") Rule was VACATED IN ITS ENTIRETY, nationwide, by the Eighth Circuit on 8 July 2025 in Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC (No. 24-3137), on procedural grounds — the FTC skipped required rulemaking steps. It never took effect (was due 14 Jul 2025). DO NOT build to the vacated rule as a legal requirement, and do not assume federal preemption of anything.
What survives federally: the pre-1973 mail/telephone negative option rule, ROSCA (Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act), and the FTC's general Section 5 authority to attack deceptive negative-option marketing case by case. The FTC has continued bringing individual enforcement actions.

STATE: roughly 30 jurisdictions have auto-renewal statutes that look like the vacated federal rule, so the practical compliance bar is unchanged. The binding constraint is the STRICTEST STATE, and that is California.
- CALIFORNIA (AB 2863, eff. 1 Jul 2025) — see the California subtask for the full requirement list: unbundled clear-and-conspicuous consent, covers free trials, 3-year consent recordkeeping, annual reminder, same-channel click-to-cancel.
- NEW YORK, COLORADO — comparable regimes; NY GBL § 527-a requires conspicuous disclosure and easy online cancellation.
- Many state ARLs are enforced through UDAP statutes, most of which DO carry private rights of action — this is why ARL claims are so common.

PRACTICAL CONCLUSION: build one national subscription flow to the California AB 2863 standard and you clear essentially every state. Two engineering artifacts are non-obvious and get missed: (1) durable storage of the consent proof for 3 years / 1 year post-termination, whichever is longer; (2) the annual reminder email job.

ONE CROSS-CUTTING DESIGN RULE: keep the biometric consent and the subscription auto-renewal consent as two separate, independently-recorded affirmative actions. Never one checkbox, never bundled into the ToS.

subtasks.title: Draft the consent + retention spec engineering can actually build
subtasks.description:
SINGLE NATIONAL BUILD SPEC. Design principle: build ONE flow to the strictest standard (Illinois BIPA + Colorado + Washington MHMD + Maryland minimisation) rather than 51 variants. Geo-gating consent by state is a trap — IP geolocation is unreliable, users travel, and residency is what matters, not location at signup.

1. THE CONSENT SCREEN (blocks the camera from opening)
- A dedicated, standalone screen. Not the ToS. Not the privacy policy. Not a pre-ticked box. Nothing else on the screen but this.
- Must state IN WRITING, on-screen, before capture: (a) that a biometric identifier — a scan of face geometry — is being collected and stored; (b) the SPECIFIC PURPOSE (identity verification at account signup); (c) the SPECIFIC LENGTH OF TERM for which it will be collected, stored and used (state a concrete period, e.g. "deleted within 24 hours of successful verification, and no later than X"). BIPA 15(b)(2) requires purpose AND duration — a vague "as long as necessary" fails.
- Affirmative action to proceed: an unticked checkbox plus a distinct "I consent" button. Electronic signature is expressly valid under BIPA as amended in 2024.
- Name the third-party ID-verification vendor and state that the scan will be transmitted to them (BIPA 15(d) / MHMD sharing consent).
- No dark patterns: consent button and decline button must be equally prominent. WA MHMD invalidates consent obtained through "deceptive design"; several comprehensive laws do the same.
- SEPARATE from the subscription auto-renewal consent. Two distinct actions, two distinct records.

2. CONSENT RECORD (the artifact you will need in litigation)
Persist, per user, immutably: user ID; timestamp; the exact VERSION of the consent text displayed (store the rendered text or a hash + versioned copy); state of residence as declared; the affirmative action captured; app version; and the vendor named at the time. Retain the consent record even after the biometric data is deleted — you must be able to prove consent for the 5-year BIPA limitations period. Retain ARL consent proof for 3 years or 1 year post-termination, whichever is longer.

3. RETENTION AND DELETION — the highest-leverage risk reduction in the whole project
- RECOMMENDATION: do not retain the face template at all. Verify, match, then delete the biometric template within 24 hours of verification completing, keeping only a non-biometric boolean ("verified: true"), the timestamp, and the method. If you hold no biometric data, most of BIPA 15(a)/(e), CUBI's destruction duty, and the entire CCPA breach class-action theory (which requires biometric data to be exfiltrated) shrink dramatically.
- If product insists on retaining for re-authentication or fraud reuse, the CEILING is the strictest of: purpose satisfied OR 3 years since last interaction, whichever is first (IL); 1 year after purpose expires (TX); whatever the published policy says (IL/CO — failing to follow your OWN policy is itself a violation).
- Build an automated deletion JOB with logging, not a manual process. Log every deletion. The absence of deletion evidence is what turns a defensible case into an indefensible one.
- Deletion must propagate to the vendor, to backups, and to any derived embeddings. Note IL 15(a) requires destruction "absent a valid warrant or subpoena" — a litigation hold does not excuse the schedule generally.

4. PUBLIC WRITTEN POLICY (a distinct document, not a paragraph in the privacy policy)
- Publish a Biometric Data Retention and Destruction Policy, publicly accessible without login. Required by IL BIPA 15(a) and CO § 6-1-1314. Colorado additionally requires it to cover BREACH RESPONSE, so include an incident-response section.
- Separately, WASHINGTON requires a STANDALONE Consumer Health Data Privacy Policy with its own dedicated link on the homepage — it may NOT be merged into the main privacy policy. This is the single most commonly missed item in MHMD compliance.
- Main privacy policy must add: sensitive-data categories, retention periods per category, the CA "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information" link, and state-specific rights sections.

5. HARD PROHIBITIONS — no consent cures these
- NEVER sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from biometric data (IL 15(c), CO, TX, and MD bans sale of sensitive data outright even with consent).
- NEVER use the scans to train models or for any secondary purpose. That breaks purpose limitation everywhere and fails Maryland's "strictly necessary" test.
- NEVER disclose to third parties beyond the named verification vendor without fresh consent.

6. VENDOR CONTRACT FLOW-DOWN (the ID-verification provider)
Required terms: process only on our instructions and only for verification; no retention beyond our stated period; no use for vendor's own model training or product improvement; deletion on our instruction with written certification; security standard at least as protective as ours; breach notice within a fixed short window; audit/assessment cooperation; MHMD processor obligations (a processor that exceeds instructions becomes a regulated entity in its own right); flow-down to sub-processors. Confirm where the vendor stores templates and for how long — vendor default retention is a very common source of unknowing violation.

7. DOCUMENTATION GATES BEFORE FIRST SCAN
- CCPA/CPPA risk assessment under 11 CCR § 7150(a) — must be COMPLETE before processing begins, because processing sensitive PI is "significant risk" processing. Producible to the CPPA/AG within 30 days of request.
- Data protection assessments for the comprehensive-law states (VA, CO, CT, etc. — one well-written assessment can satisfy most, they are broadly reciprocal).
- Security: encrypt templates at rest and in transit, strict access control, logging. IL 15(e) and TX both require care at least as protective as for your other confidential data, and CCPA's breach PRA turns a security failure directly into statutory damages.

8. MINORS
If under-18s can sign up: BIPA requires the written release from the minor's LEGALLY AUTHORIZED REPRESENTATIVE, not the minor. Colorado SB 24-041 adds consent requirements for under-18 data. Several comprehensive laws treat minors' data as sensitive per se. Simplest answer: block under-18 signup, or gate the face scan behind verified parental consent.

9. ALTERNATIVE VERIFICATION PATH (recommended, legally material)
Offer a non-biometric alternative (document upload with human review, or micro-deposit/knowledge-based verification). Two reasons: (a) it strengthens the argument that biometric consent was "freely given" rather than coerced, which matters because "freely given" is an element of valid consent in most comprehensive statutes; (b) pending bills in Mississippi and Missouri would prohibit conditioning service on biometric consent outright, and an alternative path future-proofs the product against that.

subtasks.title: DECISION: do we retain the face template at all, or delete within 24h of verification?
subtasks.description:
This is the single highest-leverage decision in the entire compliance project and everything else depends on it. Option A (recommended): delete the biometric template within 24 hours of successful verification, keep only a non-biometric 'verified: true' flag + timestamp + method. Option B: retain for re-authentication or fraud reuse.

Why A is dramatically cheaper: if you hold no biometric data you largely escape BIPA 15(a)/(e) storage duties, CUBI's destruction obligations, and — critically — the CCPA private right of action for data breach, which requires biometric data to actually be exfiltrated ($100-$750 per consumer per incident, no proof of harm needed).

If Option B, the retention ceiling is the strictest of: purpose satisfied OR 3 years since last interaction whichever is FIRST (Illinois), and 1 year after the purpose expires (Texas). Product needs to justify the business case against that exposure.

Owner: needs Product + Eng + whoever owns risk. Everything in the consent screen copy depends on the answer, because BIPA requires you to state the specific retention term on screen.

subtasks.title: Build the standalone biometric consent screen
subtasks.description:
Dedicated screen, blocks camera access until completed. Must display in writing before capture: (1) that a scan of face geometry is being collected and stored; (2) the specific purpose (identity verification at signup); (3) the specific length of term of collection/storage/use — a concrete period, not 'as long as necessary'. Name the third-party verification vendor and disclose transmission to them.

Unticked checkbox + distinct 'I consent' button. Decline option equally prominent (dark patterns invalidate consent under WA MHMD and several comprehensive laws). MUST be separate from the subscription auto-renewal consent and separate from ToS acceptance.

Electronic signature is expressly valid under BIPA as amended by SB 2979 (Aug 2024), so an in-app e-consent flow is sufficient — no wet signature needed.

Blocked by the retention decision, since the retention term has to be stated on screen.

subtasks.title: Build the immutable consent-record store
subtasks.description:
Per user, persist: user ID, timestamp, the exact VERSION of consent text shown (store rendered text or hash plus versioned copies), declared state of residence, the affirmative action captured, app version, vendor named at the time.

Retain the consent record even after the biometric data itself is deleted — you must be able to prove consent throughout BIPA's 5-year statute of limitations (Tims v. Black Horse Carriers). Separately retain auto-renewal consent proof for 3 years or 1 year post-termination, whichever is longer (California AB 2863).

This is the artifact that decides a BIPA case. If you cannot produce the exact screen a specific user saw on a specific date, you effectively have no consent defence.

subtasks.title: Build the automated deletion job with audit logging
subtasks.description:
Automated, not manual. Must propagate deletion to: primary store, the verification vendor, backups, and any derived embeddings or feature vectors. Log every deletion event with timestamp and user ID.

Note the compliance trap: under Illinois BIPA 15(a) and Colorado § 6-1-1314, failing to follow YOUR OWN published retention policy is itself a violation. So whatever the published policy says, the job must actually do — a policy promising 24-hour deletion with a job that runs weekly is worse than no policy.

Deletion logs are the evidence that converts an indefensible case into a defensible one.

subtasks.title: Publish the Biometric Data Retention & Destruction Policy
subtasks.description:
A distinct public document, accessible WITHOUT login. Legally required by Illinois BIPA 740 ILCS 14/15(a) and Colorado CPA § 6-1-1314. Must contain a retention schedule and destruction guidelines.

Colorado additionally requires the policy to cover BREACH RESPONSE, so include an incident-response section — a policy drafted only for Illinois will fail Colorado.

Must match what the deletion job actually does.

subtasks.title: Publish the standalone Washington Consumer Health Data Privacy Policy
subtasks.description:
Washington My Health My Data Act (RCW 19.373) requires a SEPARATE consumer health data privacy policy with its OWN dedicated link on the homepage. It may NOT be folded into the main privacy policy — merging them is itself the violation, and this is the most commonly missed MHMD requirement.

Must cover: categories of consumer health data collected, purposes, categories of sources, categories of third parties and affiliates with whom it is shared, and how consumers exercise their rights (access, withdraw consent, delete).

MHMD has a private right of action via the Washington Consumer Protection Act, so this is not a low-stakes document.

subtasks.title: Renegotiate the ID-verification vendor contract with biometric flow-down terms
subtasks.description:
Required terms: process only on our instructions and only for verification; NO retention beyond our stated period; NO use for the vendor's own model training or product improvement; deletion on instruction with written certification; security at least as protective as ours; breach notice within a fixed short window; audit cooperation; MHMD processor terms (a processor that exceeds instructions becomes a regulated entity in its own right under RCW 19.373); flow-down to sub-processors.

FIRST ACTION before drafting: ask the vendor in writing where face templates are stored, for how long, and whether they are used for the vendor's own model training. Vendor DEFAULT retention is one of the most common sources of unknowing violation — you can be perfectly compliant in your own stack and still be liable for what your vendor keeps.

subtasks.title: Complete the CCPA risk assessment BEFORE the first California face scan
subtasks.description:
HARD PRE-LAUNCH GATE, not a 2027 problem. Under the CPPA regulations effective 1 Jan 2026, 11 CCR § 7150(a) requires a business to COMPLETE a risk assessment BEFORE initiating any processing activity involving 'significant risk' — and processing sensitive personal information (which biometric data is) is such an activity. Because we launch after 1 Jan 2026, the assessment must exist before the first scan.

The CPPA or California AG can request a copy at any time and we must produce it within 30 days. Annual summary reporting to the CPPA begins 1 Apr 2028 for assessments conducted in 2026-27 (submit summary information, not the full assessment).

Efficiency note: write this once and reuse it as the data protection assessment for Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut and the other comprehensive-law states — their DPA requirements are broadly reciprocal.

subtasks.title: DECISION: block under-18 signup, or build verified parental consent?
subtasks.description:
If minors can sign up, Illinois BIPA requires the written release from the minor's LEGALLY AUTHORIZED REPRESENTATIVE — the minor's own consent is legally worthless. Colorado SB 24-041 (eff. 1 Oct 2025) adds consent requirements for under-18 data. Several comprehensive laws treat minors' data as sensitive per se. Arkansas HB 1717 (eff. 1 Jul 2026) adds COPPA-style teen protections.

Building compliant verified parental consent for a face-scan flow is expensive and awkward. Blocking under-18 signup is far cheaper if the product can tolerate it.

Owner: Product, with legal sign-off.

subtasks.title: DECISION: ship a non-biometric alternative verification path?
subtasks.description:
Recommended. Offer document upload with human review, or micro-deposit / knowledge-based verification, as an alternative to the face scan.

Two reasons this is legally material, not just nice-to-have: (1) 'freely given' is an element of valid consent under most comprehensive privacy statutes, and conditioning access to the entire product on biometric consent is the weakest point in our consent posture — an alternative path largely resolves it; (2) pending BIPA-style bills in Mississippi and Missouri would PROHIBIT conditioning provision of a service on biometric consent, which would break a mandatory face-scan signup outright.

Cost is real (document review ops). Decide with eyes open rather than discovering it in a legislative session.

subtasks.title: DECISION: are we launching in Illinois at day one?
subtasks.description:
The one genuinely go/no-go call. Illinois BIPA is the only biometric statute with a broad private right of action and fee-shifting, it has a 5-year lookback, and it requires NO proof of injury (Rosenbach v. Six Flags). Statutory damages $1,000 negligent / $5,000 reckless per person plus attorneys' fees.

The 2024 amendment (SB 2979) helps: damages are now capped at one recovery per person per violation type rather than per scan, and the Seventh Circuit held in 2026 that this applies retroactively. So the Cothron per-scan doomsday scenario is gone. But 100,000 Illinois signups with a defective consent flow is still ~$100M of theoretical exposure.

RECOMMENDATION: launch in Illinois, but only AFTER the consent screen, consent-record store, deletion job and published retention policy are all live and verified by counsel. Do not launch nationally-minus-Illinois as a permanent strategy — Illinois is 4% of the US market and the same build satisfies every other state anyway, so the marginal cost of compliance is low and the marginal cost of exclusion is high.

If you need to ship before the build is ready, geo-excluding Illinois by declared residency (not IP) for a short window is defensible. Excluding by IP is not — residency governs, and Illinois residents travel.

subtasks.title: Book outside privacy counsel to review the consent flow before launch
subtasks.description:
Specifically needed for four judgement calls that should not be made in-house:

1. Whether our face-scan flow is 'strictly necessary' under Maryland MODPA — consent cannot cure this test, so it is the one state where a wrong answer is unfixable by better UX.
2. Whether Washington My Health My Data applies to identity-verification biometrics. Biometric data is enumerated at RCW 19.373.010(8)(b)(ix) as a category of 'physical or mental health status', but the umbrella definition still requires the data to identify health status. This is UNTESTED and it determines whether we face a private right of action in Washington. Get a written opinion.
3. Whether conditioning signup on biometric consent breaks 'freely given' consent under the comprehensive statutes.
4. Sign-off on the consent screen wording against BIPA 15(b)(1)-(3).

Ask for a firm with actual BIPA defence experience, not general privacy advisory — the plaintiff bar in Illinois is specialised and you want someone who has seen the complaints.

subtasks.title: Build the subscription flow to California AB 2863 standard
subtasks.description:
Separate workstream from biometrics, same launch gate. The FTC 'click-to-cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED nationwide by the Eighth Circuit on 8 July 2025 (Custom Communications v. FTC), so there is no federal rule — but ~30 states have equivalent statutes and most are enforced through UDAP laws that DO carry private rights of action. California AB 2863 (eff. 1 Jul 2025) is the strictest, so build to it once and you clear the country.

Requirements: clear-and-conspicuous UNBUNDLED consent to the auto-renewal (covers free trials / free-to-pay conversions); retain proof of consent 3 years or 1 year post-termination whichever is LONGER; annual reminder notice stating renewal frequency, amount charged and cancellation instructions; cancellation through the SAME channel used to sign up, at least as easy as signing up, with a real cancel button for online signups and no obstruction flows.

Two items that always get missed: the durable consent-proof storage, and the annual reminder email job.

CRITICAL INTERACTION WITH BIOMETRICS: the auto-renewal consent and the biometric consent must be two separate, independently recorded affirmative actions. One combined checkbox violates BIPA (which needs a standalone release) and AB 2863 (which needs unbundled renewal consent) simultaneously.

subtasks.title: Set a calendar reminder to re-check the biometric legislative watch list each session
subtasks.description:
BIPA-style bills WITH private rights of action have been introduced in New York (statutory damages $1,000/$5,000, mirrors BIPA closely), Massachusetts, Vermont, Maryland (HB 33), Kentucky, Mississippi, Missouri and Washington. Any one of these passing changes the risk map materially, because private rights of action are what create class-action exposure.

Two specific things to watch for: (a) the Mississippi and Missouri drafts would BAR conditioning provision of a service on biometric consent, which would break a mandatory face-scan signup; (b) the New York and Washington drafts extend to public-sector entities.

Also re-check: Connecticut's threshold drops from 100,000 to 35,000 consumers in July 2026, and Rhode Island's 35,000 threshold is the lowest in the country — both will pull us into scope earlier than the other states as we grow.

Set this for the start of each state legislative session (most convene January).
